Pizarro 1 , 2 , 3 , Loïcka Baille 7 , Robin Cristofari 8 , Aymeric Houstin 7 , Daniel P. Zitterbart 7 , Claudia Ulloa-Contreras 1 , 2 , 3 , Gonzalo Barriga 3 , 9 , Elie Poulin 3 , 10 & … Juliana A. Vianna ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-2330-7825 1 , 2 , 3 Show authors Scientific Reports volume 15 , Article number: 29499 ( 2025 ) Cite this article Save article View saved research 6040 Accesses 10 Citations 24 Altmetric Metrics details Abstract An extensive survey for the detection of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza virus (HPAIV) H5 in seabird species is reported here. It was conducted between December 2023 and January 2024, in thirteen breeding sites spanning from the northeastern sector of the Antarctic Peninsula to the Ross Sea, including the coasts of the Bellingshausen Sea and the Amundsen Sea. Nine individuals from Pygoscelis adeliae and Leucocarbo bransfieldensis tested positive for RT-PCR amplification of a H5 segment of HPAIV in two different locations on the Antarctic Peninsula. This study suggests the possibility of the first cases of HPAIV H5 in the Antarctic continent, potentially adding two new species to the list of infected species. It also highlights the southernmost suspected cases identified to date of surveillance, and notably, no cases were detected between the Antarctic Peninsula and the Ross Sea. Ecology Genetics Health care Microbiology Risk factors Introduction The Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Virus (HPAIV) subtype H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b rapidly spread across continents within a two-year period starting from 2020, facilitated primarily by wild bird movements 1 . As the new H5 HPAIV outbreaks continue to rise, the impact on wildlife has become significantly more severe 2 . In Chile, it was detected for the first time in October 2022 3 . Given its close proximity to the Antarctic continent and the migratory movements of birds between both regions, transmission is highly likely, causing a significant threat to the Antarctic wildlife. Antarctic wildlife is highly threatened by various factors, and the current outbreak of H5 HPAIV poses a significant conservation challenge. The challenge is exacerbated by the limited monitoring of avian influenza surveillance in birds, making it more difficult for researchers to track and control the spread of the disease and the establishment of effective preventive measures. Moreover, colonial nesting seabirds are particularly vulnerable to disease transmission due to the high population density during the reproductive period 4 , 5 . These circumstances significantly increase the threat to their health and population stability. Although H5 avian influenza virus from other lineages have been reported in seabirds in Antarctica before 6 , 7 the HPAIV subtype H5N1 has never been reported up to 2023. In October 2023, a sudden and marked increase in strandings and mortality was noted among Skuas, Kelp Gulls, Elephant Seals, Gentoo Penguins and Fur Seals in Falkland/Malvinas, Bird Island and South Georgia 8 ( https://falklands.gov.fk/agriculture/avian-influenza ). Recent studies have confirmed the detection of HPAIV on the Falkland Islands and South Georgia during the 2022–2023 season 8 and in the Antarctic region, specifically on James Ross Island in the East Antarctic Peninsula, during the 2023–2024 season 9 raising significant concern. During December 2023 and January 2024, we conducted extensive epidemiological surveys of seabird nesting sites across the Antarctic Peninsula, Weddell Sea, and West Antarctica, including Bellingshausen, Amundsen, and Ross seas. We report our findings here, highlighting both the presence of suspected cases and the absence of detections in certain regions, providing critical insights into the status of avian health in Antarctica during the 2023–2024 season as well as a starting point for tracking the geographical spread of the virus in the 2024–2025 season. Methods From December 2023 to January 2024, thirteen seabird breeding sites were visited along the East and West coasts of the Antarctic Peninsula and the West Antarctica (Fig. 1 ), aboard Le Commandant Charcot icebreaker (Fig. 2 a). The laboratory is well-equipped with freezers (−80 °C,−20 °C, 4 °C) and two chambers, one designated for preparing the RT-PCR mix under sterile conditions with UV sterilization capability, and an additional chamber for exclusive use to RNA extraction (Fig. 2 b). Throughout the RNA extraction and RT-PCR setup processes, all necessary sterility and biosafety measures were strictly followed. The advanced laboratory equipment along with the high stability of the ship in harsh marine conditions ensures the reliability of the results avoiding cross contamination and false positives. A total of alive 115 birds from four species Emperor Penguin, Adélie Penguin, South Polar Skua and Antarctic Cormorant ( Aptenodytes forsteri , Pygoscelis adeliae , Stercorarius maccormicki and Leucocarbo bransfieldensis) were captured, sampled, and released (see Table 1 for species and sample sizes). The procedure was conducted considering the recommendations provided by Biological Risk Assessment of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza Virus in the Southern Ocean of SCAR 10 . A cloacal swab sample was obtained from each of the captured individuals. Samples were preserved in denaturant Viral Transport Medium (VTM). Once onboard, samples were stored at 4 °C and processed within 2–4 h of arrival at the lab, then preserved at −80 °C after RNA extraction. Subsequently, remaining RNA aliquots in VTM and extracted RNA were transported at 4 °C (on ice) to Santiago, Chile. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile (approval ID: 200624022) and the Ethics Committee of the Instituto Milenio BASE (approval ID: 4/CBSCUA/2022). All methods were carried out in accordance with relevant institutional, national, and international guidelines and regulations. Fig. 1 Full size image Sampling sites. Suspected cases are denoted in red triangles and negative cases in yellow circles. The orange dashed line shows the ship track followed. RNA was extracted using HiBind RNA Minicolumns (RNA extraction Omega) and amplified by RT-PCR against segment 4 of HPAIV H5, with specific primers AH5−918F (5’-CCARTRGGKGCKATAAATC−3’) and AH5-R1618 (5’- GAGCACATCCATAAAGATAGA−3’), with an expected amplicon size of 782 bp. The primer was designed using sequences from birds in Chile, specifically targeting the hemagglutinin (HA) gene of H5N1 HPAIV clade 2.3.4.4b (e.g., A/Pelican/CHL/226924−1/2022(H5N1), GenBank accession: OQ455466.1), and adapted to cover circulating South American variants. It does not amplify Asian strains, which are not currently present in South America or Antarctica. Historically, only low pathogenic H5 viruses had been detected in Antarctica, with two reports from the same location and year 6 , 7 and no evidence of persistence. Both studies indicate that it was a new introduction, and that the virus did not persist in Antarctica. This suggests that any H5 detected will likely be from the current outbreak. However, since late 2023 and into 2024, multiple detections of highly pathogenic H5N1 have occurred in sub-Antarctic islands and continental Antarctica. RT-PCR conditions were retrotranscription at 45 °C for 30’, followed by denaturation of 95 °C for 3’, and 40 cycles of 95 °C for 15’’, 52 °C for 30’’, and 72 °C for 60’’, followed by final extension of 72 °C for 10’. The procedure was repeated and confirmed three times for the suspected cases and randomly chosen negative cases, with a blank control included for each PCR run. Importantly, the sixteen Adélie Penguins sampled in Beagle Island were also equipped with Argos satellite trackers within the framework of another study (Le Bohec, unpublished data ), which allowed us to assess their fate in the period following sampling. Results Of the 115 individuals sampled, nine tested suspected for RT-PCR amplification, including 8 Adélie Penguins ( Pygoscelis adeliae ) and one Antarctic Cormorant ( Leucocarbo bransfieldensis ), corresponding to a prevalence of ~ 12% for all the penguins sampled. Almost all suspected cases were detected in Beagle Island, in close proximity to Danger Islands, at the northern tip of the Antarctic Peninsula. Nearly half of the Adélie Penguins sampled here were suspected for RT-PCR amplification. Another Adélie Penguin was tested suspected at Red Rock Ridge on the West Antarctic Peninsula, south of the Antarctic Circle in Margaret Bay. No suspected cases were detected in the other sixty four samples collected in the western part of the Bellingshausen Sea, in the Amundsen Sea, or in the Ross Sea. At the time of sampling, none of the birds sampled, including the suspect cases, showed evident clinical signs associated with influenza infection. Crucially, the seven Adélie Penguins that tested suspected in Beagle Island and carried an Argos tracker were still alive and engaged in foraging behavior as of early March 2024, over two months after they were tested. Agarose gel-electrophoresis confirmed the presence of PCR amplicons of the expected size for HPAIV H5 in suspected cases and their replicates, while replicates of negative cases consistently yielded negative results (Supplementary Fig. 2 ). Full size table Discussion The first-time detection of suspected cases of HPAIV H5 influenza in penguins and cormorants in the Antarctic continent could mark a significant expansion of the panzootic into this isolated continent and puts highly vulnerable bird populations at risk. The HPAIV circulating in the subantarctic and Antarctic regions indicate that the virus likely spread from South America, facilitated by the movement of migratory birds 8 . Migratory and kleptoparasite species, such as Skuas, have been proposed as the primary potential transmission pathway for the virus 11 . However, virus dynamic outbreaks can evolve and develop mutations that increase their transmissibility, but determining whether a variant becomes more prevalent due to biological advantages or epidemiological factors is complex 12 . Our findings were the first to alert the possible presence of the virus in two new Antarctic resident species, the Adélie Penguin and Antarctic Cormorant. Banyard et al. 8 confirmed a positive H5N1 case in a Black-Browed Albatross ( Thalassarche melanophris ) from the Falkland Islands and in a South Georgia Cormorant ( Leucocarbo georgianus ) from carcasses found dead. While our research covered a significant area of West Antarctica, the suspected cases so far seem to be limited to the Antarctic Peninsula, particularly in Beagle Island and Red Rock Ridge, based on our sampling. Sampling in extreme, remote, and hard-to-access conditions presents significant challenges, particularly when working with RNA viruses, which are highly prone to degradation, especially under fluctuating temperature conditions 13 , 14 . Upon arrival in Chile, some viral fragments were successfully amplified but could not be fully sequenced, likely due to RNA degradation during transport. Similarly, Banyard et al. 8 were unable to recover the complete viral sequence from all HPAIV-positive samples identified via qRT-PCR. It is now evident that the HPAIV virus has reached the Antarctic continent, being detected in other locations. Confirmed and sequenced cases of Skuas were reported from the northeastern Weddell Sea sector, specifically on James Ross Island 9 . Other cases were detected in Skuas and Sheathbills ( Chionis albus ) in Heroína Island 15 . Almost all new detection has been recorded in close proximity to the area reported in this study. There is thus significant apprehension regarding the further spread of the virus, due to the high density and mobility of these birds and their gregarious reproductive behavior - two traits that enhance intra and inter-colony virus spread, and that are thought to have largely worsened the HPAIV panzootic in Northern Hemisphere seabirds 16 . During the sampling, we did not detect any evident clinical signs in those birds potentially infected with HPAIV H5N1. There was no mass mortality event at the sampled sites, despite a positivity rate of approximately 50% among Adélie Penguins sampled by us on Beagle Island. This result suggests that certain seabird species may exhibit varying levels of susceptibility to H5 infection. Previous studies indicate that susceptibility or response to HPAIV H5N1 may vary across bird species 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 . According to Morris et al. 21 the neuro-inflammatory response varied between different bird species, having species with higher viral loads and delayed immune response timing, which are factors that affect the HPAIV H5N1 susceptibility and mortality. After our sampling, unusual mortalities of Adélie Penguins were observed at Beagle and Heroína Islands in Antarctica between March and April 2024 15 . Northworthing, in our results (Table 1 ), the higher rate (43.75%) was at Beagle Island and in the same species ( Pygoscelis adeliae ), which could be representing the initial phase of HPAIV H5 outbreaks. These asymptomatic cases may seem reassuring for the species in question, but they have strong implications for Antarctic wildlife in general, potentially leading to unnoticed and widespread virus transmission, as asymptomatic carriers could serve as “trojan horses,” facilitating the introduction and spread of HPAIV to previously unaffected populations. The absence of detected cases of HPAIV H5 between the Antarctic Peninsula and the Ross Sea is a critical finding in this study, as it suggests that, despite the virus presence in the Antarctic Peninsula, it has not yet spread to other major seabird colonies along the western Antarctic coast and into the Ross Sea. These results provide an important baseline for monitoring the future progression of HPAIV in Antarctica and underscore the need for continued surveillance to better understand the dynamics of its spread and the factors limiting its distribution. These new findings emphasize the pressing need to monitor and surveil emerging diseases in vulnerable Antarctic seabirds. Implementing rigorous biosecurity measures during Antarctic activities is essential to minimize the potential spread of HPAIV Therefore, it is crucial to focus research efforts on studying potential differential selection signals between species, evaluating immune and inflammatory response genes that may be involved in the response to this emerging disease.
